#8177. Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 26, 2026 2:00 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer. “Look at all the tracks you’ll see with snow covering the ground,” they chorus.

I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.

Hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are. And tracks may not necessarily indicate where deer are likely to be again. One deer can make a lot of tracks.

But if you know how snowfall changes a whitetail’s daily routine, you are starting to understand where you will find tracks — and the deer that made them.

First, snow normally comes late in most states’ deer seasons. That means whitetails already have been harassed by other hunters. Unless you hunt private land, all deer you are likely to encounter may be wary, even downright spooky. They are moving little during daylight hours. Rutting bucks are probably limiting much of their roaming to the darkness of night.

Second, snowstorms — and most other storms — are accompanied by periods of intensely low barometric pressure. Whitetails tend to roam wide in search of food prior to a storm. But they hole up when snow actually starts to fall. And they stay holed up until the storm passes or at least until it eases off.

Third, while snow means hunters can see deer moving much more easily, it also works the other way around. Deer see the hunter coming a lot farther off. The fact that snow silences the woods forces deer to use their eyes more. Ever spend an hour or two watching a band of deer bedded down after a snowstorm? Their heads are lifted much more often to eyeball the surrounding terrain. Eyes must assume a vigil which ears can no longer accomplish and must provide the essential early warning. Incidentally, your own hearing abilities aren’t helped by snowfall, either. Deer that rustled the crisp frozen leaves of a frosty fall morning won’t be heard walking through a soft cover of new-fallen snow.

Fourth, snow changes whitetail eating habits — particularly heavy snowfall. Meadow grasses may not be pawed at again until spring. Buds, twigs and surviving leafy vegetation take its place. These plants are less nutritious for deer but they are easier to obtain. Waste grains in fields blown clear of snow may promote a concentration of feeding whitetails.

So now you are thinking that snowfall might not be such a boon to hunting?

Actually, it is — if you know how to use it to your advantage.

Whitetails, like all wildlife, are creatures of habit. You can predict a deer’s general reaction to things that impact on its environment. Maybe your predictions won’t be precise but they can be close enough to cut down on the number of fruitless hunting efforts you make.

Pay attention to the weatherman. Be sure you are out hunting on the day before a storm is forecast to arrive. Through changes in barometric pressure, deer sense the oncoming storm. They often move out to feed as heavily as possible — even in the middle of the day — forgoing the usual bedding hours in their hasty urge to stock up before the storm. So be sure to hunt all day.

Pre-storm is the time to concentrate on checking food sources for whitetails. Hunting pressure earlier in the season may have forced the animals to visit open grainfields only at night. If hunter numbers have dwindled — as they do in most states after the first four or five days of the season — start checking those fields again at dawn and dusk. The urge to fill up before a storm may have deer less cautious.

In woodland areas, check hidden openings or meadow edges where wild herbaceous cover remains. Don’t overlook timber cuttings where saplings provide cover and the lack of an overstory promotes the undergrowth that deer savor. Try the creek bottoms where frost may not have killed the green grasses yet.

In farmlands, glass the local hay fields or even vegetable patches where potatoes, sugar beets, carrots, turnips or other root-type plants have not all been harvested yet. And visit abandoned orchards where fallen fruit may provide an attraction.

More than once in a late deer season afternoon, while driving the back roads of farm country near where I live, I have become aware of more and more deer suddenly appearing where few were before. The back edge of a cutover hay field will hold five or six deer, all feeding near a heavy hickory and oak woodlot. Harvested cornfields may have a few animals wandering along, plucking up the waste dumped by corn pickers before it can be plowed under.

Does tend to move farther from cover than bucks, particularly when feeding in daylight hours prior to a storm. But expect surprises. Once, while walking across a partially harvested cornfield to reach a gun blind in the woodlot beyond, I stumbled across a fine eight-point buck. This lone deer, feeding in a 12-row patch of standing corn, was fully 80 yards from the nearest heavy cover. He evidently felt safe among the withered cornstalks. And their rattling in the wind had probably masked the sound of my approach.

I was so startled, in fact, that I never got off a shot from the slug-loaded 12-gauge that I was carrying. The buck wheeled and bounded away before I could shoot.

Don’t be caught unprepared. You never know where a deer will suddenly appear. I’ve had does dart from brushy drainage ditches — deep ones that were mostly dry or had the damp patches frozen solid by late fall’s icy weather. Ditches provide perfect cover routes to reach open stretches with food. Shelterbelts do so, too.

Once a storm of some magnitude starts, deer simply disappear. Whitetails of both sexes will head for the thickest most protective cover around. Conifers are ideal (pine plantations or cedar swamps in the North Country). In farmlands, overgrown brushy woodlots or thick river bottom or creekbottom cover is an alternative. Here deer will lie down and, unless disturbed by a hunter wandering around in the storm, they will not get up for hours — maybe days.

The hollow hair in deer’s coats provides superb insulation from the snow’s cold and dampness. Curled up into a small oval (judge for yourself how compactly a whitetail can curl up by the sizes of the beds you’ll find a day or so later) deer will ride out the storm, sometimes allowing the snowfall to almost literally cover them. They don’t seek food and they don’t move much — even to stand and stretch.

Because hunters don’t normally slog around in heavy storms, deer are usually undisturbed until the snowfall begins to lessen. If a storm lasts more than a day, deer may move around close to their bedding areas but they won’t venture far.

It is an ideal time, once the storm begins to subside, to mount a deer drive.

Pinpointing whitetail cover won’t be difficult, even with the lack of tracks on new-fallen snow. Just pick the heaviest thickest junk around. Match the size of the cover to the number of drivers and standers you have with you, and you should be able to fill several tags for your group.

There is a farmland county near my Michigan home which is a mixture of cedar swamp, brushy woodlots and grainfields, plus some pastureland. Every other season or so, myself and about five of my hunting buddies drive over there on a Saturday. At this time, we’ve all just come back from the North Country’s season opener; perhaps half of us have been fortunate enough to have scored on a buck already. The lucky ones drive for their less successful counterparts.

Through the years, we have secured hunting permission by telephone and by long acquaintance with the local landowners, some of whom join us for these drives. Because this area is open to the use of high-power rifles, it takes only about three or four standers to cover all downwind and sidewind exit routes in the cover we visit.

The remainder of us cast back and forth in a line — more or less — of drivers, working silently in the belief that noise startles deer even more than human scent and sends them into headlong flight. We want the whitetails to break cover in a nervous trot, glancing back over their shoulders, not fleeing at top speed.

Because the drivers move and the deer focus their attention on them, the standers get some easy shots. Standers are urged to find natural blinds that will camouflage just a bit of the brilliance of the Blaze Orange garments they wear.

Drivers wear as much Blaze Orange as possible for high visibility. They don’t carry firearms, either, on our drives.

Such minidrives have proved extremely successful. In those years when we all fill tags up north and don’t plan to visit this county, local landowners call us to see if we’re coming over to help them. It has become a social event. We do go, of course.

Well-conducted drives, frankly, are one of the best ways to kill whitetails all season long — early or late, in snow or without it. If you develop a compatible group of hunters who are all safety conscious, driving may well be the best way to hunt.

For the single hunter, stillhunting in the snow can prove difficult. The muffling effect snow has on sounds is appealing to stillhunters but they should remember that whitetails bedded in snow can be extremely watchful. That’s true at least while a storm is waning or before the sun reappears with warmth enough to prompt more movement of deer. Whitetails scan their surroundings intently. And because they are not likely to be moving, spotting them will prove that much tougher.

If a stillhunter is extremely patient and slow moving, maybe he has a chance. But the average hunter who enjoys some success stillhunting on bare ground may find snowy days beyond his capability.

There is another factor making things tougher: wind. Snowstorms are often accompanied by high winds, ones that don’t die off when the snow stops falling. Wind makes all wildlife nervous. Their hearing isn’t as useful. Add that problem to the noise-muffling effect snow already has and you come up with doubly watchful whitetails.

So what about doing what you sometimes hear old-timers describe? Just plant yourself on a big buck’s track and walk him into the ground.

Unless you are a true woodsman, which most of us have neither the time nor the inclination to be, forget it. It sounds rather romantic, as the old sporting books told it, but the method isn’t likely to be very rewarding for the hunter of average skill. Oh, it can be done. And every so often you could be lucky enough to actually walk up on a buck — if you can first figure out which tracks belong to bucks and which belong to does. No, the average lone hunter faced with a snowstorm is better off doing just what the deer do: Wait it out.

Once the storm passes, whitetails will begin to circulate once again. Hunger drives them from their beds but sunny weather after a storm seems to invigorate deer, too. No scientific facts back up this phenomenon and I claim no insight into the psychology of deer. It’s just a gut feeling I have about whitetails based on observations of the ways yearlings almost cavort after a storm passes. Young bucks, not part of the serious breeding process that is probably about over when snow begins to fall, seem to want to spar. They push each other around rather good naturedly. The older does concentrate on finding food. Now’s the time for the smart single hunter to be on his stand or in his blind.

Surprisingly, there’s little need to hurry in the morning, either. Deer must feel the cold to some degree because they seldom stir at the crack of dawn after a very cold night. That fact doesn’t mean a hunter shouldn’t be out before daybreak — as he would be earlier in the season. Some whitetails may be stirring. But many times after a storm I’ve witnessed deer waiting until the sun was shining full upon them, waiting for an hour or more after daylight, before moving out to feed. It’s as if they were lying there, soaking up the warmth of the sun.

As a result, deer will often be feeding — or moving to and from feeding areas — in the middle of the day after the return of good weather conditions. For the man in a blind, deer moving on snow in full daylight are easy to spot.

Remember, also, that bedding areas on southern exposures — places where the effects of the warm sun are felt the most intensely — will be favored by deer. Anytime the temperature is under 35°, deer seem to prefer places where the sun can hit them in the morning. If it is out of prevailing winds, so much the better.

Unlike the majority of Western mule deer, which must move from higher mountain summer range to the valleys each winter, whitetails normally find everything they need to survive in a year-round home. One exception is Michigan’s Upper Peninsula where deer summering in the Lake Superior watershed tend to wander southward toward the more temperate climate of Lake Michigan in late fall and early winter, often before deer season ends. Snowfall prompts even greater movement.

A few of these whitetails travel quite a distance — 40 or maybe 50 miles. Some don’t move at all but take their chances in the deeper snowfall and reduced winter food conditions of the northern watershed. If you are aware of such a migration where you hunt, take advantage of it. The routes traveled are not always as predictable as the game trails muleys use to move downhill but various general routes are used year after year. Spot blinds accordingly.

The best advice for winter stand hunting, I think, is to stay put and to stay as comfortable as possible. Dress to remain warm in below-freezing temperatures. Make sure that your blind is well situated and that it is constructed in such a way that it blocks out any stray winds. Get a back rest and sit on a patch of canvas or plastic to keep the snow from soaking through.

I always make sure that I have a Thermos of hot coffee, tea or cocoa handy. A blind means you can move around a little without being seen and a few gulps of warm liquid can brighten a dreary day.

And be patient. Deer won’t move as often or as far in snowy weather — unless it’s a bright warm day with temperatures rising above freezing. If you are hunting alone, be prepared to wait them out. And do it in a place where they’re likely to be: near a food source or along (or in the midst of) the heavier cover where they’re certain to bed down.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

Winter hunting doesn’t have to be a case of survival against the elements. You can be comfortable and successful and see more than just tracks.

This story, “Snowstorm Whitetails,” appeared in the December 1983 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8175. The Boyhood Deer Hunt That Turned Jim Carmichel Into a Gun Guy

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 26, 2026 6:00 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

When I was a skinny, big-footed kid in grammar school, I had the unbelievably good luck of being yanked out of school for several days to go on a deer-hunting vacation with my family. Nowadays, thanks to the game commission’s deer stocking and management programs, deer are plentiful in the mountains of east Tennessee, but in the 1940s they were nonexistent. That meant that going on a real deer hunt involved traveling hundreds of miles and visiting places as far removed from our farm as was the back side of the moon. It was, to my mind, an elegant adventure, sort of like going to Europe or taking an ocean cruise. Nothing could be finer. My chums were green with envy.

Our hosts were old family friends who had struck it rich and bought an historic plantation in Virginia, complete with antebellum mansion and miles of sweet-scented hardwood forest.

On the day we arrived, dressed in our Sunday best, in a gleaming pickup truck, our host had shot a nice buck and it hung in the smokehouse. I remember inspecting the animal in elaborate detail; feeling the texture of its hair, looking at its teeth and bones and, most of all, marveling at the wonder of its gracefully curved antlers.

Horns, as they grew on cows and bulls, were familiar to me. But antlers were something entirely different — harder, more graceful and certainly more dangerous looking. I nearly lost my senses when told they were shed and regrown every year. For a while I simply didn’t believe it and only gradually allowed myself to be convinced.

And deer could jump, too, higher than a cow or even a horse. My imagination reeled with stories of these wonderful animals.

“Come on,” I said, “nothing can jump a high-wire fence.” So my host took me to a crossing place and showed where the deer-tracked path led up to a fence then continued on the other side. “Wow, they really can do it. Wait till I tell Mom.”

Next day, after breakfast of deer loin, rich gravy and biscuits, I stood in front of the gun rack, itching to get my hands on a genuine deer rifle and go hunting for these wonderful animals. Already, visions of great stags were dancing through my head.

My dad took the first rifle, a Model 99 Savage in .250 caliber, and my brother selected a shortened .30/40 Krag. Why, I wondered, had he passed over a truly beautiful Model 141 Remington pump-action rifle in .30 Remington in favor of the Krag? Anyway, I liked the pump and was glad I had a chance to use it. But when I was clear of the barn lot and stopped to load the rifle, his motives became clear. Nearly all of the cartridges had a sharp indentation on the primer, meaning they had previously misfired and were now useless. Of the lot, only three had virgin primers, and these I fed into the rifle with the optimism of youth.

Less than an hour later, I “jumped” a deer literally in his bed. He came up so close to me that for a moment I was so startled I almost turned and ran. He was not the stag of my dreams but he did have antlers, perhaps six points, and he could be mine! At first the buck ran away so fast that it looked as though I wouldn’t have time for a shot, but then he did something that still has me wondering. After running dead away for about 100 yards, he spun around and headed right at me. Clearly, he would pass by within a few feet, and even at full tilt I’d have a fairly easy shot.

Closer he came and the rifle was at my shoulder, my teeth clinched against the fearful recoil, eye squinted over the sights.

“Hurry, he’s getting away. Try another shot!”

Then the buck whirled again and headed back at me again! He was passing by close enough to hit with a hoe handle.

Tears streamed down my cheeks. Tears of disappointment, tears of frustration and tears of anger. I’d had a better than fair chance and lost it because of grown-ups who’d palmed off a bunch of useless cartridges on me. On the way back to the house, I tried the last cartridge but like its brethren, it only clicked in dismal failure.

It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

As it turned out, I was the only hunter who’d had a “shot” that day, meaning that on the following morning the gun rack was again emptied of all workable deer rifles. All that was left was a little Mossberg Model 151 Rimfire Autoloader complete with a 4X scope (don’t ask how I remember these details, how could I possibly forget?) and several boxes of Super-X ammo.

The day before, I’d passed a newly disked and seeded field of winter wheat that was covered with crows. Surely they would be there again. “If I can’t shoot a deer, at least I’ll shoot some crows,” I told myself as I lifted the .22 from the rack and pocketed a box of ammo.

The crows were there, within easy range, but my first shot kicked up dust far to the left and lower than where I’d aimed. When the crows settled back I missed again the same way. Clearly the rifle didn’t hit where the scope aimed. Why? The rest of the day, and the days following, were spent unraveling the mysteries of sight adjustment and bullet trajectory. A whole new world of excitement lay before me. So many things to learn about guns and only a lifetime to study them.

It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

A small boy can do worse than go deer hunting, even with a rifle that won’t work.

Every time I look at the 12-point whitetail mounted on my trophy room wall, I wonder if I’d do it over again if I had the chance.

It was December ’77 and I was after big whitetails on the Guajolota (translates to female turkey) Ranch in deep south Texas. When I say big whitetails, I don’t mean just big, but big-big, Texas-big, the kind of big that makes vaqueros (cowboys) whisper “muy grande” in wide-eyed wonder. The Guajolota is a working cow ranch but, like most big spreads in south Texas, it swarms with quail and so many big-antlered whitetails that owner Jim McAllen got the idea that he could make more money “farming” deer than beef.

So true to his stock-breeding tradition (McAllen, Texas, is named after Jim’s pioneer family), he set out to make his herd of deer bigger and better by using the same selective breeding techniques proven in the development of superior beef herds. In Texas, just about everyone who hunts deer either owns land, leases hunting rights or hunts on a “pay per day” ranch. (That “per day” arrangement is not the same sort of operation as the exotic game ranches, which also flourish in Texas.) Accordingly, McAllen figured that if he could breed a “super” race of elk-headed whitetails, hunters would just naturally pay more to hunt on the Guajolota.

The first step in his program was to kill off the “culls” — bucks with skimpy antlers and a tendency to pass on this trait — and save the giant bucks for a while for breeding. The program had been in effect only a few years when I hunted the Guajolota, but signs of its success were abundant on my first morning of hunting.

Accompanied by my pal Jim Nolen, maker of the well-known Nolen knives and guided by Ed Dutch, who at that time was the ranch’s game biologist but has since become a top wildlife photographer, we hid under a mesquite tree where we could look out over a 60-yard flat of open grassland.

With a bit of imagination, you might call the south Texas terrain “brush country,” but it’s not the kind of brush hunting one gets in, say, Pennsylvania or Missouri. Just about everything that grows wild in that part of the Texas empire either sticks, scratches bites or poisons, so stalking deer through the cactus and catclaw isn’t all that much fun. That’s why hunting is usually done from a quick stand or from a high seat that lets you look over the thorny chaparral. Fortunately, there is a high buck-to-doe ratio that makes the bucks especially aggressive and eager to challenge other bucks for available does.

The sound of these bucks doing battle is a distinctive clicking and rubbing of antlers that can be heard a pretty fair ways and has the effect of calling other bucks to join the fray. If you ever happen to come upon a couple of bucks fighting it out over some does, you’ll probably spot one or two more waiting their turn, and while the fighting is going on, a smarter-than-average Romeo may be trying to make off with the harem.

Many years ago, some deer hunters had the clever idea of banging a couple of deer antlers together to imitate the sounds of a fight and thereby call bucks to the gun. It worked like a charm and “rattling” up bucks has become an accepted form of the hunting arts.

I’ve tried rattling bucks from Maine to California but the only places I’ve had much success were in areas of dense deer population where there were plenty of aggressive bucks. South Texas is the home of rattling, with both the terrain and temperament of the bucks ideally suited for the technique. The trick, though, in addition to knowing how to rattle the antlers together, is finding a stand that gives you a fairly good view of at least an acre or so of relatively open space.

Some bucks apparently lose all reason at the sound of a fight and dash right in where at any other season they would fear to tread. Some rattlers report having snorting bucks right in their laps after only a moment or two of clicking the antlers. Wiser bucks will come in more cautiously, perhaps circling the stand, wanting to get sight or wind of the combatants. Thus, if you position yourself on the edge of a clearing, you get to see the deer before he gets too close. This also gives the deer a bit of breathing room so he won’t have to get too close and overly spooky. You’ll see deer heads poking out of the bush around the clearing, ears forward, and too curious — or determined — to bound away. More often than not, there’s time for a well-aimed shot, but be sure to keep your rifle close to your shoulder and ready to fire. If they see you move, they’re gone in a flash. Man, deer or fowl, there’s something about poaching on another’s territory that makes any male more than a little spooky.

Greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed.

I settled back against the forked trunk of the mesquite tree with my rifle resting on my knees. It was a trim little .250/3000 bolt gun stocked by Don Allen and built on a Mauser action that had been shortened a full inch by ace metalsmith Ron Lampert. Nolen, who was to take first turn playing the antlers, was just to my right and Dutch, who wanted some pictures, was a few yards behind, manning a telephoto lens.

Results were almost immediate. Nolen had banged the antlers no more than twice, twisting and rubbing them together to make the characteristic scrape-click-scrape sound of fighting deer when there, right in front of me, snorting and stomping his feet, was the biggest whitetail buck I’d ever seen on the hoof. He was huge, with perfectly symmetrical antlers. The main beams seemed to grow straight out in a horizontal line before hooking in at the tips. His points stood straight up like rods in an iron gate and the whole picture was a deer-hunter’s fantasy. The buck of a lifetime, too big to be true, perfect. It had to be a lie, a tale told in a deer camp, vividly remembered.

But he was there, stomping, snorting, beautiful. All I had to do was put the crosshairs on his chest and touch the trigger and my whitetail-hunting days would be over, for never would I see a bigger buck. For long moments, I held the crosshairs on his chest, poised to shoot, listening for the click of Dutch’s camera, Click-click-click it went. Now I had a record of the moment, a deer hunter at the gates of paradise. Every nerve in me howled “pull the trigger, pull the trigger,” but I didn’t.

Greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed. “Look old boy,” it said to me, “this is only the first deer. Think about the really big ones that are waiting back there in the thicket. We’ve got lots of time to wait for the absolute world beater.”

Incredibly, I lowered my rifle, worked the bolt and emptied the chamber. Then, settling the crosshairs back on the buck’s chest, I tickled the trigger.

“Just wanted to know what it felt like to pull the trigger on a giant buck,” I explained to an absolutely astonished Jim Nolen.

“Waiting for something bigger,” I allowed.

“That’s as big as they get,” was his answer, and I knew greed had done me in.

That morning we rattled in a couple more trophy-size bucks, but nothing nearly so grand as the first, so I couldn’t bring myself to raise the rifle. That afternoon, after a lunch of chili and frijoles served on a tortilla, cowboy-style, followed by a siesta, we tried again — but the antlers were cold and nothing answered the challenge.

That evening a few of McAllen’s vaqueros stopped by the bunkhouse for cerveza and conversation. “It is true,” they asked, “you had El Macho Grande in your sights and did not shoot? Why?”

I really couldn’t answer, but one thing for sure, if I ever saw him again I would shoot.

Next day the antlers were still cold, so by midafternoon we changed tactics and climbed into a tower where we could watch for deer crossing a narrow sendero (a rough, clear-cut roadway). The view from the tower allowed us to look down into the endless thicket, but no deer were moving. By early evening I had counted dozens of javelina, the small wild pigs of the Southwest, and had seen more quail than I thought existed, but no deer other than an occasional doe.

The sun hung low over the deep Texas thicket and a soft haze had wrapped itself around the evening air when the buck stepped into the sendero. The distance was just a bit more than 200 yards, but even with my 7X binoculars, the antlers were hard to judge because the sun was behind the deer, reflecting through the haze so that the deer seemed to be the center of a psychedelic burst of rainbow color. It was not a vision of earth, but a dream in pastel colors with quail calls for background music.

The buck moved slowly, a step at a time, nibbling shoots of greenery. But his antlers remained a mystery. We could see that they were big and exceptionally high, but the way they reflected shafts of gilded light made rational judgment impossible.

“I can’t see his antlers clearly,” Nolen whispered, “but I can see points everywhere.”

The buck was nearly across the sendero now and in a moment he would be gone, perhaps forever. I’d already let the trophy of a lifetime slip through my fingers. Did I dare risk losing a second chance? My trigger finger tightened and the little rifle spoke gently to the soft evening.

The buck was a freak, wearing incredible antlers that had grown to typical, though huge, shape on the right side but with an oddly palmated branch on the left. Is it the trophy of a lifetime, a one-of-a-kind specimen never to be duplicated? Or just a freak with outsize antler growth? I wonder. I wonder every time I look at it on the wall.

In addition to liberal season and bag limits, Alabama has some of the biggest-antlered and heaviest-bodied whitetails I’ve ever looked at. One Alabama trophy deer I saw a few years back got me so excited that I spent several consecutive seasons there trying to bring home the granddaddy.

And I saw lots of bucks, some eight and 10-pointers with such seductive racks that I was often tempted to touch the trigger. Patience prevailed, though, and as days turned to weeks I became more or less accustomed to the sight of the Alabama sun setting over a hardwood thicket in which, from a tree stand, I might be glassing from two to six big-antlered bucks at one time. But as I said, I wanted only the he-coon of the hardwoods and nothing else would do.

How was it, then, that I eventually shot a little eight-pointer?

Hoping to relieve the tedium of my daily wait-and-watch routine, I got myself invited to a party hunt, and on the appointed morning found myself in the midst of an incredible spectacle. The setting was a beautiful Southern mansion complete with curving driveway and vast, oak-bordered lawns. What made the scene so bizarre was the unbelievable variety of humanity strolling or squatting about the neatly clipped grounds. Tweed shooting jackets and English riding boots mixed with faded overalls and run-down clodhoppers while the elegant accents of aristocratic Southern speech were punctuated with the staccato “patoos” of well-aimed tobacco juice. There had been a violent thunderstorm during the night, and judging by the smells of wet wool and soaked leather, many of the attendees had passed the night in the rain.

A metal tub about the size of a horse watering trough was being set up on a stone foundation, eventually to be filled with gallons of cooking oil, and nearby a wild-eyed chap was tugging at a heavy chain leash in a futile attempt to separate two snarling dogs. “Get back,” he yelled when I approached to help, “these dogs are killers.”

“Then why don’t you leave them alone?” I asked.

“I’m trying to keep them from killing each other until Big Bob wakes up.”

“That’s him over yonder,” he responded, waving his free hand in the direction of an inert form stretched out in the tangled remains of what appeared to have once been a rose garden.

I meant to take a closer look, but at that moment a silence fell over the assembly as a spry black man of uncertain vintage, his hair a fluffy white, came down the brick-paved path leading from the big house.

“Mista William is a commin’,” he chanted. “Mista William is commin’, here he come now.”

Sure enough, there was the great one himself, Mister William, owner of thousands of acres of prime farmland and hardwoods, home to the biggest whitetails to be found anywhere. Obviously, Mister William had reached that unique station in society where elegant or even proper attire was no longer required as an emblem of station or success. Accordingly, he was outfitted in soiled chino work pants and shirt, the tail of the latter flapping loosely about his backside, muddied work shoes with, as I remember, only one sock and crowned off with an ancient straw hat that was liberally ventilated with odd-size holes. Yet there was no denying his regal presence. As he puffed unsteadily along the brick pavement, pausing occasionally to scratch, spit or realign his direction, there was a chorus of salutations and more than a few caps were doffed.

“Mornin’ Mista William.” “Fine day Bill.” “Good to see you Mista Bill.”

Each greeting was received with a wave and every face was recognized by name.

“Glad to see you, Jack.” “Nice of you to come over, Pete. How’s Mary and the kids?” “Hi Ralph.”

When at last he faced me, his eyes narrowed, searching for a name.

“Nice to meet you sir. I’m Jim Carmichel and I appreciated the invitation to your deer hunt.”

“Glad to have you, glad to have you,” he gestured grandly. “This hunt ain’t much, just something me and the boys like to do every year about this time.

“Hey there you, Jake, tell Big Bob I said to put Mr. Carmichel here on the road where the deer cross.”

With that he ambled back up the walk, mounted the porch steps and turned to face the breathless assembly. “Boys, the hunt’s on.”

The next few moments were lost in a bedlam of shouts, cheers, running feet and spinning truck tires. Seated in the back of a pickup (I almost made the fatal mistake of climbing into a truck full of savage curs) that fishtailed out of the driveway in a shower of mud and gravel, I caught a glimpse of Mister William as he turned and re-entered the great house, aided by his white-topped butler. Apparently he was not attending his own hunt.

Positioned as I was, on a muddied logging road, I could hear the baying pack of Catahoula curs as they topped a ridge nearly a mile away. As the baying grew louder, it was apparent they were coming my way and would cross the road in front of me. Mister William had indeed given me the best stand on the hunt and in just a few moments I would have a shot.

I was using a borrowed shotgun loaded with No. 000 buckshot and the deer would be crossing from right to left, a dead-easy setup. When the deer broke from cover and bounded across the road, I swung the bead some two feet ahead of his chest and was tightening on the trigger when I realized that it wasn’t much of a buck. An eight-pointer, perhaps, but it was a bucket-head without much width, height, or thickness of beam. The buck certainly wasn’t the world-beater I wanted. With another bound, the young buck disappeared into more timber.

By then the road was covered by a blanket of howling and snarling beasts with their owner, Big Bob, not far behind.

This was the first time I had had a close-up look at Big Bob and he was, to be sure, an awesome apparition. Clad only in bib overalls and a white T-shirt, despite the chill of the day, Big Bob stood a good six or eight inches over six feet and was as wide as a church door. His hair, probably waist length, was knotted behind his head in the style of a samurai warrior, and when he spoke I could see that every tooth in his head was covered in gold. His bout with the rose garden had criss-crossed his arms and face with bloody lacerations, and at his side swung a hunting knife that looked as long as a Saracen scimitar.

As he strode toward me — eyes wild, face blood-caked and mouth flashing of gold — the sword banged against his knee. It was the only weapon he carried. Considering his size, the obvious strength of his hands and arms and the fierceness of his countenance, the knife was more of an affectation than a necessity.

“Where’s the deer?” he asked. “I didn’t hear you shoot.”

“How come? His tracks is right there in front of you.”

At this, his eyes narrowed, “Mister, we ain’t huntin’ trophies, we’re huntin’ meat. We got a lot of people to feed tonight and if you don’t shoot somethin’ these dogs get meaner than they already are.” Big Bob made his point very convincingly.

“The next time something comes by, I’ll be sure to shoot,” I promised.

And that’s exactly what I did. A couple of hours later, the howling pack came by again in violent pursuit of a distinctly undistinguished little eight-pointer.

That evening, my buck and two others that had been killed during the hunt were sliced into bite-size chunks, rolled in batter and deep-fried in the gas-fired horse trough I’d noted earlier.

In time, huge platters were stacked with the delicious-smelling venison tidbits but, for some reason, no one took so much as a single bite. This struck me as curious because no one had eaten since breakfast and I assumed that everyone was as famished as I was. Not wanting to violate local custom, I decided it best not to serve myself until someone else had done so.

The reason for the holdup was soon apparent, however, when Mister William’s butler appeared and announced the immediate arrival of his benefactor. “Here come Mista William, ever’body git ready, here he come now.”

Mister William’s appearance was greatly improved; not only was he better turned out than several hours previous, but his gait was markedly steadier.

Without a word to the hushed onlookers, he marched straight to the deep-fry trough and extracted a crispy brown morsel of batter-dipped venison. For a moment he chewed thoughtfully, eyes cast heavenward. Then, with a sly smile, he made his pronouncement, “Boys, this meat is fit to eat.”

Later, food and drink in hand, I was buttonholed by Big Bob, his countenance no less ominous than earlier and his face still blood-caked from his personal war of the roses.

“If you had shot that other deer,” he allowed, “we would have had some extra meat for my dogs. Now I have to feed ’em dry dog food, which makes their bowels tight and they get meaner than ever.”

“Here,” I answered, handing him my half-emptied plate, “they can have mine.”

This story, “Whitetails I Have Known,” appeared in the September 1982 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8174. World Cup Ski Racing Is Back in Colorado. Here’s Who—and How—to Watch.

Ryan Cochran-Siegle at Copper Media Days on November 18, 2026 at Copper Mountain Resort in Copper Mountain, Colorado. Photo: @dustinsatloff // @usskiteam (Photo: Dustin Satloff)

World Cup skiing returns to Colorado this weekend as Copper Mountain hosts the Stifel Copper Cup for two days of high-speed competition. For American fans, it’s a chance to cheer on the U.S. Ski Team on familiar terrain—and to see how the country’s top male skiers stack up against a formidable international field.

The Nov. 28-29 event features men’s super-G on Saturday and giant slalom on Sunday. Saturday’s race is particularly noteworthy: It marks the first men’s speed race of the 2026-’27 World Cup season and the first domestic men’s World Cup stop of the winter.

And while the international field is loaded with star power, including Swiss superstar Marco Odermatt, there are several Americans worth keeping an eye on this weekend.

The headliner for the American men is Vermont native Ryan Cochran-Siegle, a two-time Olympic silver medalist in super-G and one of the country’s most accomplished speed specialists. He’ll make his season debut Saturday in a discipline where he’s proven he can hang with the very best.

Cochran-Siegle earned silver in super-G at the 2022 Beijing Olympics and added another silver in the team combined at the 2026 Milan Cortina Winter Games. He’s also a former World Cup super-G winner, and his combination of technical prowess and comfort at high speeds makes him America’s best shot at a podium on Saturday.

It’s worth noting that Copper’s super-G marks the first men’s speed race of the season, meaning everyone is starting from scratch in the discipline. Cochran-Siegle will have the home-country crowd behind him as he takes on a field led by Odermatt and reigning Olympic super-G champion Franjo von Allmen, both of Switzerland.

For Colorado ski fans, River Radamus’ name always elicits excitement. The Edwards native grew up skiing at Vail, where his parents were ski coaches, and has become one of the most consistent American giant slalom racers on the World Cup circuit.

Radamus, known for his aggressive skiing style, has developed into a regular World Cup points scorer and a legitimate contender when the course suits his strengths. He’s also familiar with Copper’s terrain from years of training at the resort.

Sunday’s giant slalom will be a particularly tough test, with Brazil’s Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, the reigning Olympic GS champion and Crystal Globe winner, leading the field. Odermatt and Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard are also contenders to watch.

Another Colorado connection is Kyle Negomir, a Littleton native and Ski & Snowboard Club Vail product who represents the next wave of American men’s racing. Negomir competes in the technical and speed disciplines and has been working to establish himself as a consistent World Cup presence.

With the American men looking to build depth behind established veterans like Cochran-Siegle, Negomir is one to watch as the season progresses. A strong showing on home snow would be a big step forward.

Both men’s races stream live on Peacock and NBCSN. Saturday’s super-G coverage begins at 1:45 p.m. ET, and Sunday’s giant slalom starts at noon ET, with the second run at 3 p.m. ET. Spectators can watch in person; general admission is free.

#8173. Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

Now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

“The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing big things.”

Actually, big is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a new best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

There’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

“I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a big challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”

Finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

She also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

The setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

“I just set it and left it,” she said. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

“I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she said. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty big disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”

Her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

“As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she said. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”

She never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

“I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she said. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”

The temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

Working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

“I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she said of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”

She also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling plan: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

Instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

“There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she says. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”

As Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she said.

Beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.)

And in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

“I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case said. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”

#8172. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

High on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun)

There is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

This is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

But can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

However, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a big-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

My reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

I watched The Alpinist on the big screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

But anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”

From my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

Nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

#8171. UTMB Moves to Wednesday in Major 2027 Schedule Shakeup

The 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28. The flagship Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) will start on Wednesday, August 25, Trail Runner Chamonix correspondent Doug Mayer confirmed with UTMB officials. This article was written under embargo and has been updated with additional information.

There are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running. Kilian and Courtney are the Greatest of All Time. A trailhead IPA will always be the best recovery drink. And UTMB week at the end of August in Chamonix, France, culminates with a 108-mile lap around Mont Blanc otherwise known as the eponymous UTMB.

One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.

For the past eight years, the alphabet stew of race acronyms comprising UTMB week started with the epic 300-kilometer PTL at the beginning of the week, followed by MCC (40K), TDS (148K), and YCC (a 5-15K youth event), before the three UTMB World Series Finals races: OCC (57K), CCC (108K) and finally UTMB (174K). A 15K event, ETC, was added in Courmayeur, Italy, in 2022.

There are three notable changes for next year’s event:

Race start times are expected to stay largely the same for the UTMB World Series Final races. Start times for other races will be forthcoming shortly.

Two blazing hot meteors of the global sports world are colliding head on. The International Cycling Union (UCI) Cycling World Championships are taking place in France’s Haute Savoie region—which includes Chamonix. The dates? August 24 to September 5.

And one date looms particularly large: Sunday, August 29, when the UCI elite men’s road race is scheduled to take place in the towns of Sallanches and Domancy, just a handful of kilometers from Chamonix.

After the UCI announced the dates for the world championships, President of the French Cycling Federation Michel Callot suggested that UTMB shift its dates.

UTMB couldn’t move into September, as the Mont Blanc Tunnel that connects Chamonix with Courmayeur, Italy, is tentatively slated to be closed again for maintenance starting on Monday, August 30. The tunnel is critical to the infrastructure of the race series—in fact, it was the reopening of the tunnel in March, 2002, after a tragic fire that forced a nearly three-year closure, that allowed race organizers to host the first edition of UTMB a year later.

Earlier dates presented their own challenges, too. “We would have been right in the middle of the tourist season,” Isabelle Viseux-Poletti, director of UTMB Mont-Blanc, tells Trail Runner. “In terms of visitor numbers and the number of people using the trails, that simply wouldn’t have worked. Everyone around the table agreed on that point.”

The discussions around the 2027 UTMB Mont-Blanc dates involved official representatives of the prefecture and of municipalities along the races’ courses, notably Chamonix, with its new mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, and directors of the UCI Championships. In the end, they went with the most reasonable option: juggling the flow of the events to better accommodate the regional impacts, and shifting UTMB week a day earlier to avoid a literal collision of events on Sunday, August 29.

The 2027 schedule was developed in close coordination with the office of Chamonix Mayor François Xavier Laffin. Laffin, who himself raced UTMB in 2007, came into office this past spring promising to review UTMB’s relationship with the town, with an eye towards mitigating the growing impacts of the race on the local population and the valley’s fragile alpine ecosystem.

Those two sporting event meteors have been heading towards a collision for more than a year now.

This will be the first time the UCI is holding a world championship that brings together all of its disciplines in the same place. That includes 20 events ranging from road cycling to mountain biking, para-cycling, and BMX. The overlap with UTMB in a region about the size of Rhode Island triggered a range of concerns about transportation, safety, and accommodations.

From the very beginning, the UCI worked jointly with UTMB. “We’ve been discussing this for quite a long time,” Viseux-Poletti says. ”From the outset, we’ve been working collaboratively to find solutions.”

But coordinating two significant sporting events is about much more than just aligning the dates, and UTMB officials had to wait until the UCI could share details about its needs, too. “In particular, we needed to understand their requirements regarding road access and law enforcement,” Viseux-Poletti says. Predictably, some of those decisions took months. And so, it was only in the last several months that coordinating decisions between the entities began in earnest.

Keith Byrne is one person who has watched UTMB race week play out for the last 11 years. An announcer for UTMB English broadcast, he’s taking the calendar shift in stride. “It’s pretty much going to be business as usual for us just with different days of the week,” he says.

Overall, Byrne is hopeful about the changes: “Out of some disturbance and adversity, there’s an opportunity to move forward.” He does wonder if there will be fewer spectators out on the course during CCC and UTMB.  “Wednesday and Thursday might not be the most productive days in the office,” he joked. “Because we’re going to make sure they have great live coverage to watch!”

American Emily Schmitz placed third at UTMB this last year. A year-round Chamonix resident for the past four years, she’s not particularly concerned about lower numbers of spectators out on the course. “There were so many spectators this year. Even if there are fewer, there are still going to be a lot of people out there cheering for you,” she observed. “And, regardless, you’re really focused on your race when you’re out there.”

If there’s a race winner among these changes, Byrne thinks it’s going to be OCC. And that’s just fine with him. “OCC will have way more eyes on it, falling on a Saturday. That’s great news for OCC runners.” The race has had fierce competition in recent years, with this year’s race featuring a remarkable duel among the top two women, Lauren Gregory (U.S.) and Naomi Lang (U.K.), who finished three seconds apart. “It was the first time in UTMB week history that the women’s finish got more people watching than the men’s finish,” Byrne said.

For spectators, Byrne found the silver lining. “If you’re a trail running fan and a cycling fan, this year you’ll have two events for the price of one.”

Could this schedule change-up, which further draws attention to the marquee events of the week, be a harbinger of things to come? UTMB officials are offering no clues.

It is clear, however, that juggling the schedule of UTMB’s many races opens a Pandora’s box of coordination headaches. There are three countries with whom to deal, plus regional authorities, nearly two dozen towns, and multiple public and private rescue services. Even for onlookers, it’s migraine-inducing.

UTMB officials declined to comment about whether this new schedule will remain the same in 2028. But they did say more changes are coming. Soon after the 2026 UTMB World Series Finals ended, UTMB officials and the Chamonix’s Mayor’s office began a series of meetings to address areas of concern raised by the mayor. Both parties have promised changes to address concerns. Viseux-Poletti expects the race series and the mayor’s office to jointly announce the news in about a month.

Doug Mayer is the author of The Race that Changed Running: The Inside Story of UTMB. He lives in Chamonix, France, and is the founder of the trail running tour company Run the Alps.

#8170. The Killington World Cup Is Back. Here’s Why This Weekend Matters for the U.S. Women.

Mikaela Shiffrin during Copper Media Days on November 17, 2026 at Copper Mountain in Frisco, Colorado. Photo: Matan Coll // U.S. Ski Team @matancoll (Photo: Matan Coll // U.S. Ski & Snowboard)

The Stifel Killington Cup returns to Killington, Vt., Thanksgiving weekend, welcoming some of the world’s best women ski racers back to U.S. soil. For the American women, in particular, there’s plenty to be excited about.

The two-day Stifel Killington Cup features women’s giant slalom on Saturday (Nov. 28), followed by slalom on Sunday (Nov. 29). It’s the first time the World Cup has visited Killington since 2024, when Mikaela Shiffrin crashed on a steep portion of the giant slalom course and suffered a deep puncture wound to the abdomen.

This time around, Shiffrin returns as a three-time Olympic gold medalist, the winningest Alpine ski racer in history, and one of the favorites in both disciplines. But she’s not the only American worth watching. A strong U.S. squad includes a rising slalom talent and an athlete who arrives in Vermont fresh off the biggest victory of her career so far.

There’s no question who will draw the biggest crowd. Mikaela Shiffrin has won 110 World Cup races and three Olympic gold medals, and she has stood atop the Killington podium six times, including four consecutive slalom victories from 2016 to 2019.

She arrives in Vermont following another impressive season, highlighted by a gold medal in slalom at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics. She’s also coming off an impressive stretch of technical racing: Shiffrin won her last five slalom starts, including the Olympics, and has finished on the podium in 14 consecutive slaloms dating back to February 2025.

Sunday’s race carries particular significance. Shiffrin has indicated that she’ll be selective about her slalom appearances this season, and Killington is expected to be her first slalom start of the winter. It’s a fitting place for her return to the discipline following her 2024 crash on the final pitch before the finish line on her second run. She lost control on the steep section of the Superstar course, slid into a gate, and punctured her oblique muscles. Shiffrin underwent surgery to clean and close the wound, followed by months of rehabilitation before returning to competition in February 2025.

In addition to the physical toll of the injury, the episode shook the ski racer’s confidence, and it took time for her to get back to her competitive rhythm. But in typical Shiffrin fashion, she went on to reclaim her place atop the sport, eventually adding another Olympic slalom gold medal to her collection in 2026.

If anyone can challenge Shiffrin for the spotlight, it’s Moltzan. The 32-year-old Minnesota native is coming off the best start to a World Cup season of her career, having captured her first-ever World Cup victory in the giant slalom in Sölden, Austria, on Oct. 24.

Moltzan’s breakthrough win was a long time coming. A consistent contender on the World Cup circuit, she has steadily established herself as one of America’s strongest technical racers. She also earned an Olympic bronze medal in the team combined at the 2026 Games, further cementing her place among the country’s top Alpine racers.

With confidence from her first World Cup victory and a strong history of giant slalom results, Moltzan is a legitimate podium threat on Saturday. She’ll also be one to watch in Sunday’s slalom.

Keep an eye on 25-year-old AJ Hurt, who’s emerging as another important piece of the American technical team. Hurt has been particularly impressive in slalom this season, finishing fourth at Gurgl, Austria, and 15th at Levi, Finland, earlier this month. She was the top American woman in both races.

That fourth-place finish at Gurgl was especially encouraging, putting Hurt within striking distance of her first-ever World Cup podium. She’s shown the ability to ski aggressively against the world’s best, and another strong performance in Killington could be a significant step forward.

Other American technical racers, including Nina O’Brien and Katie Hensien, are also worth following as the start lists take shape. O’Brien has established herself as a strong giant slalom competitor, while Hensien brings additional technicality to the U.S. slalom squad.

Both days of racing will be broadcast live on NBC and Peacock, with first runs available on Peacock and NBCSN. Saturday’s women’s giant slalom begins at 9:30 a.m. ET, with the second run at 12:30 p.m. ET.

Sunday’s slalom starts at 10:30 a.m. ET, followed by the final run at 1 p.m. ET. For viewers who can’t tune in live, Peacock will also offer streaming access to the races.

#8169. Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman)

When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

“All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he says. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

Later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between big walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Then he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

“At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he says. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

“The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman says. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

So Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he launched his company, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, New Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

“The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so big,” he says. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty quickly.”

The results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.)

Zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he said, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

“Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he showed up with Friends,” he says, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”

Zartman says he’s unaffected by the new competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

Zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

“Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he says. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”

Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design new testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.

“To a lot of people’s surprise,” he laughs, “I’ve sold a lot of gear.”

I’ve included a wide range of price options, with some gift ideas so big they’ll take up half your living room and others small enough to fit under the tree.

Tires are the most important overland upgrade. A good set of all-terrain tires like the BFGoodrich KO3s helps drivers safely get through snow and mud, and up and down rocky backcountry roads. Their tougher construction also helps resist flats. I love the KO3s for their legendary off-road reliability combined with their quiet ride on pavement.

Overlanders love to get stuck so they can get back out, which makes recovery gear essential. Maxtrax boards slip under tires that have lost traction, allowing the vehicle to slowly inch out of snow, mud, sand, or whatever else it’s bogged down in. Go for the more expensive Xtreme version because it comes with metal traction teeth that last significantly longer.

Airing down tires is often the easiest way to get unstuck because it increases the tires’ contact patch. I love the Rhino kit because it airs down four tires at once. I also recommend this ARB air compressor that attaches to a car battery and can reinflate the tires before you hit pavement again.

Sometimes self-recovery isn’t an option after getting stuck, and I’ve had to get yanked out by a friend. This device fits in the two-inch rear receiver on any truck or SUV and creates a safe place to attach a D-ring and recovery strap. Heads up: Make sure whoever you gift this to knows how to use it properly before heading out.

Folded down, this shovel is only 18 inches long. Fully extended, it goes to 34 inches and is perfect for digging your truck out of a snowbank or excavating a cathole near camp. I’ve tested an earlier version of this shovel for years, and the carbon steel head has put up with rocks, trees, and firm ground without ever bending or chipping.

Anyone who’s overlanding for more than a couple of days will love an electric fridge. It eliminates ice runs and keeps food from drowning in meltwater. Dometic makes some of the most reliable fridges on the market. I like this one because it has two zones: one a fridge, the other either a fridge or a freezer.

Coffee tastes better at 9,000 feet. To brew it there, Yeti’s indestructible French press is my go-to. I’ve thrown it in a kitchen box or just let it roll around in the back of my truck, and it still works perfectly every time. I also love that it has a ceramic lining so the coffee doesn’t taste like metal.

Water can be a precious commodity on a backcountry trip. That’s why I use this battery-powered faucet that pulls water from a jug and then dispenses just the right amount so I can wash my hands or do dishes. One charge lasts for weeks, and all the hoses are easy to clean at home. Pair it with a Dometic water jug for the ideal setup.

The REDARC GoBlock is my go-to overland battery (for fridges, lights, etc.) because it’s designed to be charged in multiple ways. I recommend the kit version, which includes a dock that bolts to a truck bed and gives the battery a secure place to live at all times.

iKamper nailed the details with this version of the Skycamp rooftop tent. It has the smartest mounting system I’ve tested. The bombproof hardshell cover will put up with years of sun and weather, and inside it’s extra roomy thanks to a clever tent design. It’s pricey, but this is one of those buy-once, cry-once purchases that you’ll have for at least a decade.

Two layers of enhanced memory foam make the Foamy the most comfortable camping mat on the market. Nothing else I’ve tested even comes close. Perfect for larger tents or truck beds, the Foamy almost guarantees a good night’s sleep because it’s so plush. Pair it with a camping blanket and the setup will be almost as comfortable as what you’re used to at home.
